steps: Open "Work history" and find a paused task card.
Click "Resume".
Check the task continues from where it stopped.
items.needs: a paid account and a paused Work task
items.note: Stopped tasks are not confirmed to show Resume; the code shows it for the paused state.

items.where: Work history > running task card > "Stop"
steps: Open "Work history" and find a running task card.
Click the stop button (labelled "Stop" with the task title).
Wait for the "Stopping task" spinner to finish.
Check the task state changes to stopped and the run no longer progresses.
items.needs: a paid account and a running Work task
items.note: The visible button may be icon-only; its accessible name is "Stop: <task title>".

items.where: Work session in chat > plan review > step marked "Failed" > "Retry from this step"
steps: Run a Work task until a step shows "Failed".
Open the step's menu or the plan review.
Click "Retry from this step" (also labelled "Retry a step").
Check that only that step runs again and the task continues.
items.needs: a paid account and a Work task that fails a step
items.note: I did not confirm the exact screen on which the retry control appears after a failure.

items.where: Work history > click a finished task > "Re-run this task"
steps: Open "Work history" and click a finished task (not running).
Click "Re-run this task".
Check a new chat opens in Work mode with the same goal, deliverable and constraints in the composer.
Send it and check it runs again from the start.
items.needs: a paid account and a finished Work task
items.note: The button fills a new draft; it does not start the run by itself.

items.where: Work history > click a finished task > "Re-run this task"
steps: Open "Work history" and click a finished task.
Click "Re-run this task".
Check the goal, deliverable and constraints appear in an editable composer draft in a new chat.
Edit the text and send, then compare with the original task.
items.needs: a paid account and a finished Work task
items.note: No control is named Duplicate; "Re-run this task" is the nearest and opens an editable draft.

items.where: Work history > click a finished task > "Result" section
steps: Open "Work history" and click a finished task.
Find the section labelled "Result".
Compare its text with what the task produced.
items.needs: a paid account and a finished Work task with a result
items.note: While a task is running the same section is labelled "Latest output".

items.where: Work history > click a finished task > "Outputs" section > "Download and open"
steps: Open "Work history" and click a finished task that produced a file.
Find the "Outputs · N" section.
Click "Download and open" on a file.
Check the file opens or downloads.
items.needs: a paid account and a finished Work task that produced a file
items.note: Older outputs show "Download unavailable for this historical output." instead.

items.where: Work history > click a task that stopped short > plan section with "Remaining:"
steps: Open "Work history" and click a task that stopped before its last step.
Find the line "Done N of M steps before it stopped."
Read the "Remaining:" line below it.
Compare with the steps you expected to finish.
items.needs: a paid account and a Work task that stopped short

items.where: Desktop: Sidebar > Work (opens the "Work history" page). Web: Command palette > "Work history".
steps: Sign in with an account that already has past work tasks, then click "Work" in the left sidebar.
Check that the page heading reads "Work history" and the subtitle reads "Your Cloud work sessions".
Click the filter "Active", then "Needs you", "All" and "Archived" in turn, and check that the list changes to match each filter.
Scroll to the bottom of the list and, if a "Load more" control appears, click it to load older tasks.
Click any task row and check that its detail panel opens with that task's title and state.
items.needs: a signed-in account with past work tasks; on desktop, privacy mode must not be Local
items.note: The desktop sidebar label comes from the key sidebar.nav.tasks, which reads "Work" in the English file. Load-more text and the exact row-click behaviour were not checked against a running app.

items.where: Web only: Work history > open a finished task > "Share task" (opens "Share conversation"). On the desktop Work page the button is not passed in, so it does not appear there.
steps: On the web app, open "Work history" and click a finished task row (not one that is still running).
In the task detail panel, find the button "Share task" under the source conversation line and click it.
Check that the dialog title reads "Share conversation" and that it offers a share link with an expiry choice.
Note: the dialog shares the source chat, not a separate plan or step list. Confirm whether the shared link shows the task's steps and results.
items.needs: a signed-in web account with a finished task that has a source conversation
items.note: The Share task button is hidden while the task is live, and the desktop transport does not supply shareConversation, so it is web-only. Whether a share includes the plan, steps and results as Expected says is not confirmed by the code read.

items.where: Sign in to the same account on a second device or browser, then Sidebar > Work (web: Work history) and look for the task under "Active" or "Needs you".
steps: On device A, start a work task and leave it running or waiting for approval.
On device B (or a second browser), sign in to the same account and open "Work" in the sidebar.
Find the task in the "Active" filter, or in "Needs you" if it waits for input, and click it.
Use the task's own controls (for example Pause, Resume or approve) and check that device A shows the new state after a refresh.
If a decision conflicts, check that the message reads "Another device already answered this approval." or "Another device already resumed this task."
items.needs: two devices or two browsers signed into the same account, and a running task

labels.text: Another device already resumed this task.

items.note: The task list is loaded from the account on the server, so it can show on any device, but the code read does not show whether the second device updates live or only on refresh. Two real devices are needed to confirm this.

items.where: Command+K (Ctrl+K on Windows) > type "Work history" > Work history. Then look at the list (the default filter is "Active"); "Board" is the second layout button, next to the "List" one.
steps: Press Command+K to open the command palette, then type "Work history" in the "Search chats and actions" box and press Enter on the "Work history" result.
On the Work history page, keep the filter on "Active" and check that each running or queued Work task has its own row, with a small live dot on the running ones.
Click the "Board" button in the layout control at the top right of the list.
Compare the rows or cards: several running tasks should be visible together in one view, not one at a time.
items.needs: two or more Work tasks running or queued at the same time
items.note: The overview lists all of them, but the detail panel on the right follows only one selected task at a time. The sidebar has no Work history entry; the route is /tasks, reached here through the command palette or the "Active" section on the Chat home screen.

items.where: Work history > filter "Needs you" (or the unfiltered list, where these tasks are placed first)
steps: Start two Work tasks, one that will ask for approval and one that keeps running, then open Work history from Command+K > "Work history".
With the filter on "Active", look at the top of the list: a task waiting for approval or paused should appear above the running ones.
Click the "Needs you" button in the filter control at the top of the list.
Compare: only tasks that need your input should be shown, and they should be the first rows.
items.needs: one Work task that is waiting for approval and one that is still running
items.note: The code treats awaiting_input, awaiting_approval and paused as needing input and moves those rows to the top of the list. The top-of-list placement is set in code and is not a separate visible label.

items.where: Work history > a task card showing "Waiting for your approval" > Approve or Deny buttons on that card
steps: Open Work history (Command+K > "Work history") and keep the list on the first page.
Find the task whose card says "Waiting for your approval". Optionally type a note in the box "Guidance for this work session".
Click "Approve" (or "Deny") on that card, without opening the task details.
Compare: the card should show a short busy spinner, then the task should move on, and you should still be on the Work history list.
items.needs: a Work task that is waiting for your approval
items.note: The inline unblock is for approval requests only. The "Message the agent" box in the task details panel is a separate steering control for live tasks.

items.where: Work history > click a task row > "Task details" panel > "Open source chat"
steps: Open Work history and click the title of any task row (it has an "View details for" label for screen readers).
On the right, the "Task details" panel opens with the goal, the plan, the latest output or result, and the activity list.
Scroll the panel to the bottom and read the note about events; if it says "Showing the first 4,000 events", click "Open source chat".
Compare: the chat that ran the task should open and show the conversation the task came from.
items.needs: a Work task that has already run, ideally one with more than 4,000 events
items.note: The panel shows a summary of the activity and stops at 4,000 events. The code says the full record is in the source chat, so the panel itself is not a complete transcript; the tester should check this against Expected.

items.where: Chat > open a conversation with an answer > hover under an assistant reply and click the branch icon (tooltip "Branch conversation: this chat stays unchanged"); or the conversation's "Conversation options" menu > "Duplicate as branch"
steps: Open a conversation that has at least two messages and one assistant reply.
Hover under the assistant reply and click the icon button labelled "Branch conversation from here" (or click "More message actions" on a user message and choose "Branch conversation from here").
Wait for the toast "Conversation branch created"; the app opens the new chat.
Type a new message in the new chat and send it, then go back to the original chat.
Compare: the new branch should continue on its own and the original chat should be unchanged. The arrows "Previous branch" and "Next branch" should move between versions.
items.needs: a conversation with at least one reply
items.note: The branch icon on assistant replies appears only on hover, and the "Duplicate as branch" item is shown only when the conversation has messages.

items.where: Scheduled > More ways to create a task (arrow next to New task) > Start from a template
steps: Sign in, click Scheduled in the sidebar.
Click the arrow button next to New task (aria-label "More ways to create a task").
Click Start from a template.
Look for the template gallery section titled Start from a template with ready-made routines to pick.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules (otherwise the button reads Upgrade plan); at least one saved routine, because the gallery only shows when the list is not empty
items.note: The Desktop app has the same gallery in apps/desktop/src/features/schedules/DesktopCloudSchedules.tsx, but its toggle button text was not confirmed.

items.where: Scheduled > New task
steps: Click Scheduled in the sidebar, then click New task.
Type a name in Schedule Name and the instructions in Task Instructions.
Pick a Frequency such as Daily, then click Create Schedule.
Look for the new routine card in the list with the name and prompt you typed.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules

items.where: Chat > a finished reply's menu > Run this on a schedule
steps: Send a message in chat and wait until the reply finishes streaming.
Open the menu on that reply.
Click Run this on a schedule.
Look for the schedule form opening, and check whether it carries that reply's content.
items.needs: a finished assistant reply in a chat
items.note: The exact button that opens the reply's menu and whether the form is pre-filled from the reply were not confirmed in code.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Schedule Name and Description (edit later with Scheduled > routine card > Edit Schedule)
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Type a name in Schedule Name and text in Description.
Click Create Schedule, then click the Edit Schedule icon on the routine card.
Change the name or description, click Save Changes, and check the card shows the new values.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules
items.note: Edit Schedule is a tooltip title on an icon button, not visible text.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Task Instructions (later: routine card > Edit Schedule > Task Instructions)
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Type several lines into Task Instructions, pressing Enter for new lines.
Click Create Schedule, then Edit Schedule on the card.
Look for the Task Instructions box showing all lines, edit one line, click Save Changes and check the change stays.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Sources
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Find the Sources group of checkboxes.
Tick or untick Project instructions and files, Saved memories, The web or Recent chats.
Click Create Schedule, reopen Edit Schedule, and check the same boxes are still set.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules; a project with files if you want to test project files
items.note: The Code line pointed to moved lines. The Sources group was found in ScheduleAccessFields.tsx; I did not confirm that the form renders it.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Connectors
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Find the Connectors group; wait for Reading your connectors to go away.
Tick the connectors the routine may use.
Click Create Schedule, reopen Edit Schedule and check the choice is kept.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules; connectors set up in the account to see choices
items.note: Whether the list is empty without connectors was not confirmed.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Run as agent
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Open the Run as agent drop-down; the default is No agent.
Pick an agent from the list.
Click Create Schedule and check the card or Edit Schedule shows that agent.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules; at least one custom agent created to see choices beyond No agent

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Frequency > One Time > Run At
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Set Frequency to One Time.
Pick a date and time in Run At that is in the future.
Click Create Schedule and check the card shows that one time as its next run.
items.needs: none

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Frequency > Daily, Weekly or Monthly
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Set Frequency to Daily, then set Local Time.
Click Create Schedule.
Look at the card's next-run information and check it repeats at the chosen time.
items.needs: none
items.note: Whether the card shows the repeat wording was not confirmed.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Time Zone
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Click the Time Zone field and type a city or region in Search by city or region…
Pick a zone, then set a Local Time.
Click Create Schedule, reopen Edit Schedule and check the Time Zone is kept.
items.needs: none
items.note: The Code line pointed to moved lines; the field was found at ScheduleForm.tsx line 510.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Frequency > Interval, Custom Cron or Recurrence Rule
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Set Frequency to Interval and fill Repeat Every, or Custom Cron and fill Cron Expression, or Recurrence Rule and fill Recurrence Rule.
Optionally set Only Run During to a window.
Click Create Schedule and check the card shows the advanced recurrence.
items.needs: none

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Frequency > When An Event Happens
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Set Frequency to When An Event Happens.
Look for the trigger choices: GitHub, Slack, Gmail, Google Calendar, Anything else (signed webhook).
Pick one, save, then send or cause that event and check a run starts.
items.needs: a connected account for the chosen service (for example GitHub or Gmail) to test a real event
items.note: Not confirmed whether the trigger panel is inside the form or appears after saving; firing an event was not verified in code.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Frequency > When An Event Happens > Only when
steps: Set Frequency to When An Event Happens and pick a trigger.
Find the Only when group.
Pick a field from the drop-down, or Other field…, and enter a Value.
Save, send a matching and a non-matching event, and check only the matching one starts a run.
items.needs: a connected event source to send real events
items.note: Only the field conditions were confirmed; event type, account and repeat-suppression wording was not found as visible labels.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Frequency > When An Event Happens > Anything else (signed webhook)
steps: Set Frequency to When An Event Happens and pick Anything else (signed webhook).
Save, then copy the endpoint and signing secret shown in the trigger panel.
Send a signed POST to the endpoint, using the example command shown in the panel.
Look in the routine's run history for a new run.
items.needs: a terminal to send the POST; the signing secret from the panel
items.note: The panel builds a signed curl example; the exact labels for the URL and secret were not confirmed.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card menu > Run now
steps: Click Scheduled and open the menu on a saved routine.
Click Run now.
Look for a new run in Latest result or the run history with a status and output.
items.needs: a saved routine; a routine that is finished or legacy shows Run now disabled
items.note: The button that opens the card menu was not confirmed in code.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card (next-run line)
steps: Click Scheduled and look at each routine card.
Find the next-run time (shown as a tooltip titled Next run on the card).
Compare the time with the Time Zone and Local Time set in Edit Schedule.
items.needs: a routine that is active
items.note: The label used on the card itself was not confirmed; Next run found here is the sort option text.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card (Last run line)
steps: Click Scheduled and open a routine that has run.
Look for the Last run line on its card.
If the last run failed, check the error text after Last run.
items.needs: a routine that has run at least once; a failing run to see the error

items.where: Scheduled > routine card > Latest result (run history)
steps: Click Scheduled and open a routine that has run.
Open the Latest result panel from the card.
Look for the list of past runs with status and time.
If there are no runs, check the text This schedule has not run yet.
items.needs: a routine with past runs

labels.text: This schedule has not run yet.

items.note: The control that opens Latest result from the card was not confirmed in code.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card > Latest result > a run
steps: Open Latest result for a routine that has run.
Click or open a past run in the list.
Look for the run's output text, not only its status.
items.needs: a routine with a finished run that produced output
items.note: Opening a single run and its output view was not confirmed in code; ScheduleRunHistory.tsx shows the run list.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card > Pause (or Resume)
steps: Click Scheduled and find a routine that is active.
Click Pause on its card, or Pause in the card menu.
Look for the Paused label on the card and that it does not run at its next time.
Click Resume and check the label goes away.
items.needs: a saved routine

items.where: Scheduled > routine card > Edit Schedule
steps: Click Scheduled and click the Edit Schedule icon on a routine card.
Change a field such as Frequency, Local Time or Task Instructions.
Click Save Changes.
Look at the card and reopen Edit Schedule to check the change saved.
items.needs: a saved routine
items.note: Edit Schedule is a tooltip title on an icon button.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card menu > Delete
steps: Click Scheduled and open the menu on a routine.
Click Delete.
Read the confirmation Delete Schedule? and confirm.
Look for the routine gone from the list and that it no longer runs.
items.needs: a saved routine; the deletion is permanent
items.note: The card menu that holds Delete was not confirmed in code; the dialog wording was read but its consequence text was not.

items.where: Scheduled > routine card > Share (link dialog Share “<routine name>”)
steps: Click Scheduled and open the share action for a routine.
In the dialog, copy the Share link.
Open the link in a second account in the same workspace or another browser, and check it offers to create a copy.
Check the original routine is unchanged.
items.needs: a second account to open the link
items.note: The Share menu item wording was taken from a test file, not the component; the recipient copy flow was not confirmed.

items.where: Scheduled > New task > Maximum Runs and Credit Cap
steps: Click Scheduled, then New task.
Fill Maximum Runs with a number, and optionally Credit Cap.
Click Create Schedule.
Let the routine reach the limit, or check Edit Schedule shows the cap is kept.
items.needs: a plan that can create schedules
items.note: Empty fields show the placeholder No limit…; whether all plans can set these was not confirmed.

items.where: Scheduled > (routine card) > Run History (clock icon) > run row shows "Waiting for your approval" with the approve and deny buttons
steps: Sign in and open "Scheduled" in the left sidebar.
Open a routine that uses a tool which asks for approval, and run it unattended (or wait for its schedule to fire).
When the run needs approval, the routine card shows a paused note: "Paused: a run needed your approval. Approve or deny it in Run History". Click the Run History (clock) icon on the card.
In the run row, look for the "Waiting for your approval" box listing the tool calls with an approve and a deny button, and an "Expires" time.
Click approve. Compare with Expected: the run should resume and finish, and the approval box should go away.
items.needs: a routine whose unattended run needs a tool approval (the tool's approval has to be triggered by the run)
items.note: The approve and deny button words come from TOOL_APPROVAL_ACTION_LABELS in packages/types, not a literal in these files. The desktop screen (apps/desktop/src/features/schedules/DesktopCloudSchedules.tsx) shows the same approval box under "Recent results" and asks the user to approve in run history. The code paths for pausing and resuming are in apps/web/lib/services/scheduled-agent-executor.ts and the tool-call gate; the resume after approval was not confirmed on screen, and the labels for the "resume the schedule" action were not checked.

items.where: Scheduled > (routine card) > Run History (clock icon) > run row shows "skipped" and a note such as "Skipped the run scheduled for ..." or "Ran late: scheduled for ..."
steps: Sign in and open "Scheduled" in the left sidebar.

Make sure a routine has a recurring schedule and its run was missed (for example the computer was asleep or the app was closed when it was due). The "If A Run Is Missed" setting in the routine form decides whether it runs late or is skipped.
Click the Run History (clock) icon on the routine card.
Read the run row: a skipped run shows the word "skipped" in place of the status, plus a note explaining why. A late run shows the note "Ran late: scheduled for ...".
Compare with Expected: the history should say that the occurrence was missed or skipped and why.
items.needs: a routine with a recurring schedule and a run that was actually missed (the tester cannot force this easily)
items.note: The note text is built in code (a template string), so the full sentence is not one literal; the setting label "If A Run Is Missed" is in apps/web/features/schedules/components/ScheduleForm.tsx. The desktop Recent results section (apps/desktop/src/features/schedules/DesktopCloudSchedules.tsx) also shows the same timing note. Whether a missed run is shown in a live test was not verified.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > Read the page
steps: Sign in, open a chat, and pair Chrome with the AGI extension if it is not paired yet.
Open a web page in Chrome and keep it as the active tab.
Click the + button in the message box, then click Use the browser.
Click Read the page and read the address, title and text shown in the Recent activity area and the transcript box.
Compare the shown title and address with the page open in Chrome.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser with the AGI extension and a page open in Chrome
items.note: The dialog shows the page text, but the code did not show that a question typed afterwards is answered from it.

items.where: Chrome: highlight text on an approved site > right-click the selection > Explain this, or open the AGI side panel > + > Add selected text
steps: In Chrome, open a site the user has approved in the AGI extension.
Select a sentence or paragraph of text on the page.
Right-click the selection and click Explain this.
Or open the AGI side panel, click its + button and click Add selected text.
Look in the AGI chat for the selected text sent as context and the question asked about it.
items.needs: Chrome with the AGI extension and an approved site
items.note: The Chrome-side entries were found; the handoff into the Desktop chat was traced only as far as the bridge server.

items.needs: A paired Chrome browser with a page open
items.note: No button named Summarize was found; the closest is Read the page in Use the browser, whose description mentions summarizing, and the summary request is typed in chat.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > Read the page, then type the question in the chat box
steps: Pair Chrome with the AGI extension and open a page in Chrome.
Click the + button in the message box, then click Use the browser.
Click Read the page to load the current page.
Type a question about the page in the chat box and send it.
Check that the answer uses facts from the page that is open in Chrome.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser with the AGI extension and a page open in Chrome
items.note: Whether the page text reaches the chat answer was not traced end to end.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > Open a page
steps: Click the + button in the message box, then click Use the browser.
Choose Open a page.
Type https://example.com in the field labelled Address.
Send the action with the dialog's action button.
Look in Chrome for the new address opened in the active tab.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser with the AGI extension
items.note: The dialog's action button label was not found by name; it was not confirmed.

items.where: Browser panel of a coding session (aria-label "Browser") > Back, Forward or Reload
steps: Open a coding session that shows the Browser panel and load two pages in it.
Click Back and check that the previous page loads.
Click Forward and check that the next page loads again.
Click Reload and check that the current page reloads.
Check that Back and Forward are greyed out when there is no history.
items.needs: Desktop app with a coding session and a Browser panel
items.note: The known gap holds: the assistant has no reload command, and how the Browser panel is opened from the session was not traced.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > Type
steps: Pair Chrome and open a page with a form in Chrome.
Click the + button in the message box, then click Use the browser.
Click Read the page and note a field selector from the text shown.
Choose Type, enter the CSS selector in the field labelled CSS selector and the value in Text, then send.
Look in Chrome to see the text typed into that field.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser and a page with a form
items.note: The tester must know a CSS selector; the dialog does not find fields by name.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > Recent activity
steps: Pair Chrome, then open Use the browser from the + button.
Run Read the page or Open a page.
Look at the Recent activity list in the dialog.
Check that the new entry shows the command name and its status: running, then done or failed.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser with the AGI extension
items.note: The list is shown only while the dialog is open, and it resets when Desktop restarts.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > Download a file > Downloads section
steps: Pair Chrome, open Use the browser, and choose Download a file.
Type the address of a file in the field labelled Address and send it.
Look for the Downloads section listing the downloaded file name.
Click Open Downloads folder and check the file is there.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser and a file address to download
items.note: The Downloads section appears only after a download succeeds; an approval step before download was not found in this file.

items.where: Settings > Browser > Clear browsing data > Clear
steps: In the Desktop app, open Settings and go to the Browser section.
Click Clear browsing data.
Read the confirmation titled Clear browsing data? and click Clear.
Look for the message Browsing data cleared.
Open a site that needed sign-in in the browser pane and check that you are signed out.
items.needs: Desktop app (the section is hidden on the web)
items.note: The settings nav label is taken from the section heading Browser, which was not separately confirmed in the navigation file.

items.where: Chat composer > the + button (aria-label "More composer options") > Use the browser > run an action > result text above Recent activity
steps: Pair Chrome, open Use the browser, and run an action such as Read the page.
Read the result text shown above Recent activity.
Read the Recent activity entries for the outcome: done, or failed with a message.
If an action fails, look for the message That browser action did not run.
items.needs: A paired Chrome browser with the AGI extension

labels.text: That browser action did not run.

items.note: The code shows the result and the activity status, but a written chat summary of what remains for the user was not confirmed in the dialog.

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Desktop app > Computer use > Any app
steps: Open Settings… from the app menu.
Under Desktop app, click Computer use.
Turn on the switch labelled Any app.

Look for the rows Accessibility and Screen Recording with Open System Settings buttons and compare with Expected: the permissions are shown and linked, but no step-by-step wizard was found in the code.
items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app (Electron host); no guided wizard found
items.note: Code shows a toggle plus permission rows, not a guided multi-step setup; the Expected 'guided' part looks different from the code.

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Desktop app > Computer use (with Any app on) > Accessibility and Screen Recording rows
steps: Open Settings… and go to Desktop app > Computer use.
Turn on Any app.
Read the Accessibility and Screen Recording rows: each shows what it is for and a status such as Not asked yet or Allowed.
Where the status needs action, click Open System Settings for that row and compare with Expected: each permission has a purpose line.
items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app

labels.text: Computer use: moving the pointer, clicking and typing

items.note: The same rows also appear under Desktop app > Permissions (SYSTEM_HINT text in DesktopPermissionsSection.tsx).

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Desktop app > Computer use > Allowed apps
steps: Open Settings… and go to Desktop app > Computer use, with Any app on.
Ask AGI in chat to work in an app, for example TextEdit, while Computer use is on.
When the permission dialog appears, choose the allow option it offers (Deny is the refuse button).
Go back to Computer use and look under Allowed apps for that app; each row offers Remove, and an empty list reads None yet.
items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app and one installed app to test with
items.note: The list cannot add an app directly; an app is added only through the permission dialog during a task. The session-allow button label was not confirmed.

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Desktop app > Computer use > Refused apps > Add app
steps: Open Settings… and go to Desktop app > Computer use.
Under Refused apps, click Add app (only shown when the Desktop can refuse apps).
Type in Search apps and pick an app in Installed apps.
Check that the app now appears under Refused apps, then ask AGI in chat to control it and compare with Expected: it should not run.
items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app and an installed app to refuse
items.note: Refused rows show Always refused or Refused until you quit Desktop; Ask again restores them.

items.where: Effect seen in the chat activity: Looked at display N
steps: On a Mac with two displays, with Computer use on, ask AGI in chat to take a screenshot, then ask it to look at the second display.
Open the activity under the reply and check the step reads Looked at display 2 (the number is passed by the agent).
Compare with Expected: the screenshot should come from the chosen display.
items.needs: a Mac with two displays and a computer-use task
items.note: The display choice is a tool parameter the agent sends, not a control in the UI; the id must come from a previous screenshot listing.

items.where: Chat, under the reply: activity step cards with a screenshot
steps: With Computer use on (Settings… > Desktop app > Computer use > Any app), send a chat request that makes AGI click or look at the screen.
While it runs, open the activity shown under the reply.
Look for each screen step card with a picture of the screen and the caption Screen after: followed by the action.
Compare with Expected: the picture should match what the agent saw.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on and an app to act in
items.note: A picture appears only when the step returns one; I did not confirm the exact live timing.

items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app
items.note: Searched ComputerUseSettings.tsx and ComputerUseControlBar.tsx: they show the phase text but no app name. The app name is only in step text (In front: <app>) in apps/web/features/desktop-host/lib/device-steps.ts, which the model reads. No on-screen app label found.

items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app
items.note: Searched ComputerUseSettings.tsx, ComputerUseControlBar.tsx and the step text in device-steps.ts: no window label is shown to the user. The window is read natively in apps/desktop/electron/native/macos/agi-input.swift, but no UI text using it was found.

items.where: Chat (computer use on): ask AGI to copy or paste with the keyboard; then Settings… > Capabilities > Local access > Permissions
steps: Turn on Computer use (Settings… > Desktop app > Computer use > Any app).
In chat, ask AGI to paste text into an app with Command+V.
When the dialog appears, read its reason about the clipboard and choose Deny or allow.
Open Settings… > Capabilities > Local access > Permissions and look for Read the clipboard; compare with Expected: it needs its own answer.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on
items.note: The prompt text is set in apps/desktop/electron/runtime/computerUseSteps.ts; the dialog button labels were not confirmed.

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Capabilities > Local access > Folders > Add a folder
steps: Open Settings… and click Capabilities, then find Local access.
Under Folders, click Add a folder and choose a folder in the picker.
Check the folder is listed under Folders.
Click Remove on that folder, confirm Remove access in the dialog, and compare with Expected: the folder is no longer listed.
items.needs: a Mac with the Desktop app and a test folder
items.note: Local access is a Desktop-only section shown under Capabilities.

items.where: Chat (computer use on): ask AGI to open an app, for example TextEdit
steps: Turn on Settings… > Desktop app > Computer use > Any app.
In chat, ask AGI to open TextEdit.
Allow the permission prompt if one appears.
Look for the TextEdit window opening on the Mac and compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app and an installed app to open
items.note: A missing app gives an error that names it; the exact wording was not captured here.

items.where: Chat (computer use on): send a request to click and type in an app, then the activity under the reply
steps: Turn on Settings… > Desktop app > Computer use > Any app, and open TextEdit.
In chat, ask AGI to click the New Document button and type a short word.
Open the activity under the reply and look for the step lines Clicked at ... and Typed.
Compare with Expected: the text should appear in the app.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on and TextEdit
items.note: none

items.where: Chat (computer use on): ask AGI to scroll in an app, then the activity under the reply
steps: Turn on Computer use and open a long page or document in an app.
In chat, ask AGI to scroll down in that window.
Open the activity under the reply and look for the step line Scrolled at ...
Compare with Expected: the window should scroll.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on and a scrollable window
items.note: none

items.where: Chat (computer use on): ask AGI to drag an item, then the activity under the reply
steps: Turn on Computer use and open an app with a draggable item.
In chat, ask AGI to drag the item to another place.
Open the activity under the reply and look for the step line Dragged from ... to ...
Compare with Expected: the item should move.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on and a draggable item
items.note: none

items.where: The Computer use bar: Paused. You have the screen.
steps: Start a computer-use task in chat with Computer use on.
While AGI is working, move the mouse or type.
Look for the bar text Paused. You have the screen. with the hint It paused when you moved the pointer or typed.
Compare with Expected: AGI should stop instead of fighting for the mouse. Then click Hand back to continue.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on
items.note: The bar's placement on screen was not verified in the code read.

items.where: Press Escape while AGI is active, or File > Stop Computer Use
steps: Start a computer-use task in chat with Computer use on.
While AGI is working, press Escape, or open the File menu and click Stop Computer Use.
Look for the Computer use bar to disappear, or the Stop button to turn off, and check the chat stops.
Compare with Expected: all computer control should end at once.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on
items.note: Escape is the stop key (COMPUTER_USE_STOP_SHORTCUT); the Stop button also appears in Settings > Desktop app > Computer use.

items.where: Computer use bar > Take over, or File > Take Over Screen Control
steps: Start a computer-use task while AGI is active.
Click Take over on the Computer use bar (or File > Take Over Screen Control).
Look for the text Paused. You have the screen. and the button now reading Hand back.
Compare with Expected: AGI should hold still while you use the mouse.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on
items.note: The same Take over button is in Settings > Desktop app > Computer use.

items.where: Computer use bar > Hand back, or File > Hand Back Screen Control
steps: While AGI is paused, click Hand back on the Computer use bar (or File > Hand Back Screen Control).
If a dialog titled Hand the screen back? appears, click Hand back in it.
Look for the bar to return to AGI is using your computer.
Compare with Expected: AGI should continue the task.
items.needs: a Desktop app with a paused computer-use task
items.note: The Hand the screen back? dialog is in apps/desktop/electron/runtime/computerUseSteps.ts; I did not confirm which click opens it.

items.where: Chat (computer use on): ask AGI to type into a password field or send a message
steps: Turn on Computer use and open a test app with a password field or a message box.
In chat, ask AGI to type a password or send a short message.
When the dialog titled Check this step appears, read the message that starts Desktop wants to.
Click Deny and check the step does not run, then repeat and choose Allow once and compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on and a test app
items.note: The review text comes from the agent or a password-field check (computerUseSteps.ts).

items.where: Chat, activity under the reply: the step lines
steps: Run a computer-use task in chat with Computer use on.
Open the activity under the reply.
Look for one line per action, such as Clicked, Scrolled at or Looked at the screen, and any error line.
Compare with Expected: each action should be recorded and show whether it worked.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on
items.note: There is no separate receipt screen; success or failure display in the activity was not fully confirmed.

items.where: Chat (computer use on): ask AGI to control Finder or System Settings
steps: Turn on Computer use with Any app.
In chat, ask AGI to control Finder or System Settings.
When the permission dialog appears, read the reason text about what the app can reach.
Compare with Expected: the product should say why it cannot or should not control that app.
items.needs: a Desktop app with computer use on

labels.text: Finder can open, move and delete any file you can, so controlling it reaches every file on this computer.
System Settings changes how this computer is set up, including its privacy and security settings.

items.note: Missing apps give No app called ... is installed. The refusal for a blocked app is written for the model, so the chat wording may vary.

items.needs: a cloud task with a linked computer that is offline
items.note: Found the wait notice Waiting for <computer> to come online in apps/web/lib/device-steps/device-clearance-step.ts and the wait limit in apps/web/lib/workflows/cloud-agent-workflow.ts, but did not find the screen that shows it. Searched those files only.

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Desktop app > Computer use > Allowed apps > Remove
steps: Open Settings… and go to Desktop app > Computer use.
Under Allowed apps, click Remove on an app.
Ask AGI in chat to control that app again.
Compare with Expected: AGI should stop and say how to allow it again, with Ask again or the permission prompt.
items.needs: a Desktop app with an app already allowed
items.note: The wording AGI uses after a revoke comes from the model; the code text asks the user to allow the app.

items.where: Settings… (app menu) > Capabilities > Remote Control > Pair a phone, then Copy link for a browser
steps: In the Desktop app, open Settings… > Capabilities > Remote Control and click Pair a phone.
Click Copy link for a browser.
On another device, open that link, paste it in the box on the page, and send a task.
Compare with Expected: the task should run on your own Mac.
items.needs: a paid plan, a second device, and the Desktop app
items.note: Code says Remote Control comes with paid plans. The owner's notes say it is hidden in v1 (2026-11-14), so check the build before testing.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > New > folder chip (local folder menu, "Change the folder")
steps: Sign in to the Desktop app and click Code in the sidebar.
Click New to start a session, then click the folder chip in the composer.
Pick a folder from the list in the menu.
Check that the chosen folder name stays on the chip before you send, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: the Desktop app with at least one local folder added
items.note: Cloud sessions use a "Select repository" chip instead of a folder chip; the exact composer position was not traced in the render tree.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > New > branch chip under the folder chip ("Change the branch")
steps: Open Code, click New, and pick a local folder that is a git repository.
Click the branch chip shown under the folder chip.
Type in "Search or type a branch name" or click a branch in the list, then click "Use this branch".
Check that the chip shows the branch you chose.
items.needs: a local git folder with more than one branch

labels.text: Search or type a branch name

items.note: Cloud sessions use the same "Change the branch" label for a repository branch; local switching checks out the branch in the folder.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > New > environment selector ("Local" or "Cloud")
steps: Click Code, then New.
Open the environment choice in the composer and look for "Local" and "Cloud".
Select "Cloud" and check that the composer changes to repository controls.
Select "Local" and check that the folder chip returns.
items.needs: a paid account for the Cloud option
items.note: Cloud sandbox execution is unfinished: it depends on the E2B switch (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts). Whether the Cloud option actually runs in a sandbox today was not verified; the exact selector position was not traced.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > Your computer (session list)
steps: Sign in to the Desktop app and click Code in the sidebar.
Look for the "Your computer" section and the "On this device" list.
Click a session row to open it.
Check that the session opens and its title is shown, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: the Desktop app with a folder allowed to run commands
items.note: A folder shows no sessions until its command access is allowed; the empty-state text is "No coding sessions on this device yet."

items.where: Sidebar > Code > Your computer > session row > More actions > Rename
steps: Open a session from Your computer.
Click the "More actions for" control on the session row (its name is the session title).
Click Rename and type a new name in the "Session name" field.
Check that the new title shows in the list and the session header.
items.needs: a Desktop app session
items.note: Cloud sessions also have a "Rename" item (apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts). The exact text of the More actions label was built from a function, not a fixed string.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > Your computer (status words on each session row)
steps: Open Code and look at the "Your computer" list.
Start a task in a session and watch the row change to "Running".
Wait for the run to end and check the row shows "Ready" or "Idle".
Check that a session with an archived state shows "Archived".
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a task that asks for approval
items.note: Visible copy for failed and closed states was not found in the status labels read; "Approval required" appears on the approval card (apps/web/features/code/local-code.ts), not as a status word.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > Your computer > session > Files > open a file > Edit > Save
steps: Open a Desktop app session whose folder has a text file.
Click Files (or press Command P) and open the file.
Click Edit, change a line, then click Save.
Check that the change shows in the file and that the file on disk changed.
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a text file in its folder
items.note: The exact button position in the session panel was not traced; the editor code is in apps/web/features/code/components/LocalFileEditor.tsx.

items.where: Code > local session > Terminal (also Session actions > Open in > Terminal)
steps: Open a Desktop app session.
Click Terminal, or open Session actions > Open in > Terminal.
Click the "Run a command" field, type a short command such as ls, and click Run.
Check that the output appears under the terminal.
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a local folder
items.note: The terminal is LocalTerminal.tsx; the exact dock position was not traced in the render tree.

items.where: Code > local session > Terminal (empty text "No commands have run in this session.")
steps: Open a Desktop app session and click Terminal.
Check that the empty text "No commands have run in this session." shows if nothing ran.
Run a command, then look at the list of commands with their output.
Check that each entry shows the command and its result, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a local folder

labels.text: No commands have run in this session.

items.note: The exit status is kept in LocalTerminal.tsx (exitCode) but its visible wording was not found; check it on screen.

items.where: Code > local session > Changes (the Changes panel, then pick a changed file)
steps: Open a Desktop app session in a git folder and make a change to a file (a task or an edit).
Click the "Changes" button in the session.
Click a changed file in the Changes panel.
Check that the line-by-line diff shows removed and added lines, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a git folder with a changed file
items.note: The diff renderer (CodeDiffFile.tsx, LocalChangesPanel.tsx) was not read line by line; the "Changes" button label was confirmed from the test file apps/web/features/code/components/LocalSessionPanel.test.tsx.

items.where: Code > local session > Changes (file list with commit choices)
steps: Open a session with several changed files.
Click the "Changes" button.
Look at the commit line "Commits N of M changed files" and the "Include in the commit:" choices.
Untick one file and check the count changes.
items.needs: a git folder with several changed files
items.note: The words for created, modified or deleted per file were not found in the labels read; check the file rows on screen.

items.where: Code > local session > the Permissions chip > Plan (cloud: Approval mode > Mode > Plan)
steps: Open a Desktop app session and click the "Permissions" chip (it shows the current mode, such as Ask).
Choose "Plan" and read the hint "Reads and plans. Changes nothing."
Send a request that would edit a file, and check the agent proposes a plan and does not change files.
Check the plan waits for approval before any edit, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a local folder
items.note: The hint says Plan changes nothing; the approval step after the plan was not traced.

items.where: Code > local session > the Permissions chip > Auto (or Ask)
steps: Open a Desktop app session and click the "Permissions" chip.
Read the choices: Ask, Auto, Plan, Bypass permissions.
Choose "Auto" and read the hint "Edits files without asking. Asks before commands and git hook or MCP changes."
Send a small edit request and check it edits without asking, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a local folder
items.note: The visible word is "Auto", not "agent mode". In the cloud composer the same control is labelled "Approval mode" (apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts).

items.where: Code > local session > Permissions chip (Ask / Auto / Plan / Bypass permissions); cloud: Approval mode chip
steps: Open a Desktop app session and click the "Permissions" chip.
Pick "Ask" and send a task that runs a command; check it asks for approval.
Pick "Auto", then "Bypass permissions", and send the same task.
Check the approval prompts follow each mode, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app session with a local folder
items.note: The cloud Approval mode options are Ask, Auto and Skip. Whether the running session honours each mode was not verified.

items.where: Code > composer > Usage ring button (popover shows "Context window")
steps: Open a session in the composer.
Click the small usage ring button (aria label "Usage").
Read the "Context window" line in the popover.
Send a message and reopen the popover to check the used amount rises.
items.needs: a signed-in account with an open session
items.note: The ring is UsageRing in apps/web/features/code/components/CodeComposer.tsx; it shows the context window only when the model size is known.

items.where: Code > composer > Usage ring button > "Plan usage limits"
steps: Open the composer in Code.
Click the "Usage" ring button.
Read "Plan usage limits", "Five hour limit" and "Weekly, all models", and "See detailed breakdown".
Check the bars and reset times match your plan, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a signed-in account
items.note: If usage data is missing the popover shows "Usage is not available right now." (apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts).

items.where: Code > local session > "Push and open a pull request" (on a branch other than the default)
steps: Open a Desktop app session in a GitHub-connected repository on a non-default branch.
Look for the "Push and open a pull request" action in the session.
Click it, then check the pull request number ("Pull request #") and state (open, draft, merged or closed) appear.
Open "Open a pull request on GitHub" to compare the link with the panel.
items.needs: a GitHub-connected repository, a non-default branch, and a linked GitHub account

labels.text: Push and open a pull request
Open a pull request on GitHub

items.note: Panel placement was not traced; the panel component is apps/web/features/code/components/LocalPullRequest.tsx. Some states show a reason instead when a pull request is not possible.

items.where: Code > local session > Run tests (results under "Test output")
steps: Open a Desktop app session in a folder with a test script in package.json.
Click "Run tests".
Watch for "Running <command>" and then the result line such as "<command> passed." or "<command> failed with exit code N."
Open "Test output" and check the failing output appears, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a Desktop app session in a folder with a test command
items.note: The button position was not traced in the session panel; if no test command is found, the text "No test command found here" appears.

items.where: Code > session > Session actions > Share (dialog "Share session")
steps: Open a cloud session in Code.
Click "Session actions" and choose "Share".
In the "Share session" dialog, pick the sharing option and copy the link.
Sign in with a second account in the same workspace (or open the link) and check the session opens, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a second account
items.note: Sharing options shown as "Shared with your team" and "Shared by link" (apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts). The share dialog file is apps/web/features/code/components/CodeShareDialog.tsx; the exact opening path was not traced end to end.

items.where: Code > session > Session actions > Open in > Desktop app (or Open in > Terminal)
steps: Open a session in Code in the web app or Desktop app.
Click "Session actions", then hover or click "Open in".
Choose "Desktop app" and check the session opens in the desktop app.
Check the same session is shown with the same transcript, to compare with Expected.
items.needs: a paired desktop app signed into the same account
items.note: "Continue in VS Code" also appears in the session panel (apps/web/features/code/components/LocalSessionPanel.tsx). The Desktop item shows only when a desktop is paired; the phone route was not checked.

items.where: Code > On this device > Add a folder, then New session in that folder > Start a coding task > Explore the project
steps: Click Add a folder and choose a project folder on this computer.
Click New session in that folder.
In the Start a coding task area, click Explore the project.
Read the reply. It should name the main folders, entry points and how they connect, as Expected says.
items.needs: Desktop app with a folder on this computer added
items.note: The Explore the project button sends a fixed prompt that asks for the project's purpose and main files.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Click the Continue this session box and type: Where is <function or name> implemented? Give the file and line.
Click Send.
Check that the reply names the defining file and line.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No separate control; this is a free-form question to the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Type in the Continue this session box: Where is <symbol> used across the repository?
Click Send.
Check that the reply lists references in several files.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No separate control; this is a free-form question to the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Type in the Continue this session box: Trace how <button or action> flows from the UI to the code it changes.
Click Send.
Check that the reply walks from the entry point to the final effect, with file names.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No separate control; this is a free-form question to the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Type any question about the project in the Continue this session box.
Click Send.
Check that the answer is based on the project's files.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No separate control; this is a free-form question to the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Permissions (set to Auto) > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Set Permissions to Auto. The shortcut is Cmd+Shift+M on a Mac.
Type a feature request in the Continue this session box and click Send.
Click Review changes and check that new or edited files appear.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a writable test folder
items.note: Ask mode asks before each edit, so use Auto to see edits without prompts.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Permissions (set to Auto) > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Set Permissions to Auto.
Type a bug description and the steps to reproduce it in the Continue this session box, then click Send.
Click Review changes and check that the fix touches the file that causes the bug.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a test folder with a known bug
items.note: No separate control; the fix is made through the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Permissions (set to Auto) > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Set Permissions to Auto.
Type: Refactor <module> into smaller parts without changing behaviour. Click Send.
Click Review changes and run Run tests to check behaviour is unchanged.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No separate control; the refactor is requested through the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Permissions (set to Auto) > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Set Permissions to Auto.
Type: Write tests for <function>. Click Send.
Click Review changes and check that a new test file or new test cases appear.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No separate control; tests are requested through the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Run tests (header button)
steps: Open a local session for a folder that has a test command.
Click the Run tests button in the session header.
Watch the status line: Running <command>.
Check the result: <command> passed., or failed with exit code, and read Test output.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a folder with a test script
items.note: If no test command exists, the message says No test command found here.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Run tests (header button) > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Run tests on a folder where a test fails.
Open Test output and read the failure.
Type in Continue this session: Explain why these tests fail and fix the cause. Click Send.
Check that the reply names the failing test and cause, and that Review changes shows any fix.
items.needs: Desktop app; a folder with a failing test
items.note: No separate control; the interpretation is requested through the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for a TypeScript folder.
Type in Continue this session: Run the project's type checker and list the errors. Click Send.
Check that the reply reports the checker's errors with file names, or states there are none.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a folder with a type checker
items.note: No dedicated type-check button; the check is requested through the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Type in Continue this session: Run the project's linter and list the findings. Click Send.
Check that the reply reports the lint output with file names.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a folder with a linter
items.note: No dedicated lint button; the check is requested through the agent.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Terminal panel > New terminal
steps: Open a local session for the folder.
Click the Terminal panel button in the session header.
Click New terminal and type the project's build command, then press Return.
Check that the terminal ends with the build's output and exit status.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a folder with a build command
items.note: No dedicated build button; the build runs as a typed terminal command.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Terminal panel > New terminal
steps: Open a local session and click the Terminal panel button.
Click New terminal and type the project's dev server command, then press Return.
Ask the agent in Continue this session for a small edit and click Send, while the server keeps running.
Check that the server stays up. Closing its tab should ask: Close this terminal? and say it is still running here.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a folder with a dev server command
items.note: The keep-running behaviour is partly visible in the close prompt text; the agent's own use of the server is not shown in the UI.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Browser (header button)
steps: Open a local session and click the Browser button in the header.
Click Web address, type a local URL such as localhost:3000, and press Return.
Use Back, Forward and Reload to check the pages load.
Ask the agent in Continue this session to check the page, and read the reply.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session; a running local web app for the URL
items.note: The page is shown in the Browser pane; the agent's own inspection steps are not shown in the pane.

items.needs: a paired Chrome browser for the agent step
items.note: No console panel found in apps/web/features/code/components/LocalBrowserPanel.tsx. The console step exists as device_browser_console in packages/contracts/local-runtime/src/device-steps.ts:289 for the paired Chrome browser, and the user is asked before it runs. Not confirmed as a visible control.

items.needs: a paired Chrome browser for the agent step
items.note: The network step exists as device_browser_network in packages/contracts/local-runtime/src/device-steps.ts:294 for the paired Chrome browser. No network panel found in LocalBrowserPanel.tsx.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer) > type /review
steps: Make a change in the folder, then open a local session.
Click Review changes in the header and check the changed files.
Type /review in Continue this session and click Send.
Check that the findings name file and line, as Expected says.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session that has uncommitted changes
items.note: The /review command's description, Review the changes in this session for bugs, is in apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts.

items.where: Settings > Connectors > GitHub > Review pull requests
steps: Open Settings and click Connectors.
Find the GitHub connector and turn on Review pull requests.
Open a pull request on that repository and wait for it to open.
Check that AGI posts a review as a comment on the pull request.
items.needs: A GitHub account with the AGI GitHub App installed on a repository, and a pull request
items.note: The GitHub card name is taken from the connector data and was not checked on screen. The review is posted by the GitHub webhook route at apps/web/app/api/github/webhook/route.ts.

items.where: Code > Cloud sessions > open a session > Continue (composer) > type /security-review
steps: Click Code in the sidebar and open a cloud session that has changes.
In the composer, type /security-review and pick it from the list.
Click Send.
Check that the reply lists security problems with their location.
items.needs: A paid plan with Code, and a cloud session with a repository

labels.text: Check the changes in this session for security problems

items.note: The /security-review command is in the cloud composer. Not confirmed for the local composer.

items.where: Code > open the session after a review or scan > read the reply in the transcript
steps: After S67.20 or S67.22 finishes, open the same session.
Read the reply in the transcript.
Check that each finding has a plain explanation and a file and line.
items.needs: A session that has run /review or /security-review
items.note: No separate findings view was found; findings appear in the agent's reply.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Permissions (set to Plan) > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session and set Permissions to Plan.
Type in Continue this session: Propose a fix for <issue>, do not change any files. Click Send.
Read the proposed change in the reply. Check Review changes shows no edits.
Set Permissions to Ask, ask again, and check the Approval required card with Approve and continue appears before any edit.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: The Plan mode description is in LOCAL_AGENT_MODE_HINTS in apps/web/features/code/local-code.ts.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Review changes > Stage file or Revert file
steps: Open a local session with several changed files and click Review changes.
Click Stage file on one file only.
Check the status says Staged 1 change. and that other files are not staged.
Click Revert file on another file, confirm Revert these changes?, and check only that file changes back.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session that has several changed files
items.note: Hunk-level Stage and Revert also exist. The cloud Changes panel has Include in the commit checkboxes in apps/web/features/code/code-surface.ts.

items.where: Code > On this device > open a session > Continue this session (composer)
steps: Open a local session with Permissions set to Auto.
Type in Continue this session: Write or update the README section for <module> from the code. Click Send.
Click Review changes and open the README or doc comment changes.
Check the new text matches the code.
items.needs: Desktop app with a local folder session
items.note: No dedicated documentation button; the request is made through the agent.

items.where: Code > Add a folder (if none is open) > New session in [folder name] > type the migration task and send
steps: Sign in to the desktop app and click Code in the sidebar.
If no folder is listed, click Add a folder and pick a git repository folder on this Mac.
Click New session in [folder name] under that folder.
Type a migration task, for example: Rename every use of the old config key to the new key, and send.
Look at the reply and the Changes pane: the agent names the files it changed, and those files now show the new name.
items.needs: the desktop app and a git repository folder on this Mac
items.note: There is no migration button; the agent does it from a chat request, so the tester checks the agent's output, not a control.

items.where: Code > Add a folder (if none is open) > New session in [folder name] > type the upgrade task and send
steps: Sign in to the desktop app, click Code and open a session in a folder that has a package manifest (for example package.json).
Type an upgrade task, for example: Upgrade one outdated dependency to its latest version and fix any code that breaks, and send.
Wait for the agent to finish, then open the Changes pane.
Compare: the manifest and the code files the agent changed are listed, and the agent reports the new version it installed.
items.needs: the desktop app, a folder on this Mac with a package manifest, and network access for the package registry
items.note: There is no upgrade button; this depends on the agent running the install in the folder, so the tester checks its output.

items.where: Code > New session in [folder name] > type a commit request in the message box and send
steps: Click Code, then New session in [folder name].
Type a small change request, for example: Add one line to README.md, and send. Wait for the change.
Type: Commit these changes with the message Add README note, and send.
If a commit hook runs, a prompt asks you to allow it. Answer it.
Compare: the agent reports the commit. Open Changes: a line reads Stages and reverts changes. Run git commit in your terminal to commit. when you commit by hand.
items.needs: the desktop app and a git repository folder on this Mac

labels.text: Stages and reverts changes. Run git commit in your terminal to commit.

items.note: The agent commits with its git_commit tool. The Commit message and Commit and push form is on the cloud Code page, not in a local folder session.

items.where: Code > New session in [folder name] > type a branch request in the message box and send
steps: Click Code, then New session in [folder name] on a folder that is a git repository.
Type: Create a branch named qa-branch-test for this work, and send.
Compare: the agent reports the new branch name.
Open Changes and check the branch name shown in the session group in the sidebar, or ask the agent: Which branch are we on?
items.needs: the desktop app and a git repository folder on this Mac

labels.text: Create branch and open pull request

items.note: The agent creates the branch with git_branch_create, which does not switch to it. The button Create branch and open pull request shows only when the folder is not on a branch (LocalPullRequest.tsx).

items.where: Code > [session in a folder] > Changes > Push and open a pull request
steps: Click Code and open a session in a git folder that is on a branch other than the default branch and has a GitHub remote.
Make a change with the agent so there is something to push.
Click Changes in the session header.
Click Push and open a pull request below the file list.
Compare: a Pull request # link appears with a checks status. Clicking it opens the pull request on GitHub.
items.needs: a GitHub account connected to AGI, and a git folder with a GitHub remote; without the AGI GitHub App on that repository, the button opens the GitHub compare page instead

labels.text: Push and open a pull request
Open a pull request on GitHub

items.note: The pull request block is inside the Changes pane (LocalChangesPanel.tsx); the Create branch and open pull request button appears instead when the folder is on no branch.

items.needs: none
items.note: Code line says partial: the switch-on is an E2B sandbox gate (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts). I searched apps/web for issue_comment, app_mention and mention triggers and found no UI path that starts coding from a GitHub issue or team mention.

items.where: Code > [session in a folder] > Memory button (brain icon, tooltip Memory) > What to remember > Save to memory
steps: Click Code and open a session in a folder.
Click the Memory button in the session header (brain icon, tooltip Memory).
Type a repository fact, for example: Tests run with the npm test script. Choose Project memory and click Save to memory.
Compare: the line Saved to appears with a file path.
Open a new session in the same folder and ask: How do we run the tests? The answer should use the saved fact.
items.needs: a folder on this computer, and memory turned on for the account (the Memory button is hidden otherwise and in remote SSH sessions)
items.note: The button shows only when runtimeModels.features.memory is true (apps/web/features/code/components/LocalSessionPanel.tsx).

items.where: No control. Seen in a new session in a folder that has an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file
steps: Create AGENTS.md in a test folder with one rule, for example: Always answer in one word.
Click Code and open a new session in that folder.
Ask a question such as: What is the capital of France?
Compare: the reply follows the rule from AGENTS.md. In the terminal CLI, /memory shows what the session loads.
items.needs: a folder on this computer with an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file
items.note: The instruction files are loaded by the CLI loader (apps/cli/src/compaction.rs load_instructions); the desktop app path was not confirmed in the cited dispatcher lines.

items.where: Code > [session in a folder] > Skills and plugins button (sparkle icon, tooltip Skills and plugins) > turn a switch on or off
steps: Click Code and open a session in a folder that has a skill or plugin.
Click the Skills and plugins button in the session header (sparkle icon).
If a project skill is listed and not trusted, read the note and click Trust this folder's skills.
Turn one skill's switch off, then on. Each row shows the name and its scope, under Skills or Plugins.
Compare: a switched-off skill is not used when you ask for it, and a failed change shows That change could not be saved.
items.needs: the desktop app, a folder open in a local session, and a folder or account that has at least one skill or plugin
items.note: The button shows in every local session header (LocalSessionPanel.tsx line 1067); the list is empty when no skill or plugin is installed.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > Cloud sessions > open a session
steps: Sign in, then click Code in the sidebar.
Click a session under Cloud sessions.
Note the session title and the address, which ends in /code/ and an ID.
Open the Desktop app, go to Code, and open the same session.
Compare the title and ID with the Expected line.
items.needs: an account that has a cloud session, and the Desktop app
items.note: Desktop app shows the same hosted web pages, so cloud sessions match by URL; local sessions are a separate list.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > Cloud sessions > open a session
steps: Sign in, click Code in the sidebar, and click a session under Cloud sessions.
Scroll the conversation and note the last message.
Open the same session in the Desktop app's Code view.
Compare the conversation history and the last message with the Expected line.
items.needs: an account with a cloud session that has several messages, and the Desktop app

items.where: Sidebar > Code > open a session > Changes
steps: Click Code in the sidebar and open a session that has a repository.
Click the Changes button in the session header.
Read the branch shown next to the git branch icon (base, arrow, working branch).
Open the same session in the other client and check the same branch name appears.
Compare the branch with the Expected line.
items.needs: a session linked to a git repository, and a second client
items.note: The branch name is data from the session, so the exact name cannot be taken from the code.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > open a session > header chip
steps: Click Code in the sidebar and open a cloud session.
Read the small chip in the session header: network setting, then a dot and the repository name.
Open the same session in the other client and read the chip.
Compare the repository name on both clients with the Expected line.
items.needs: a cloud session with a repository, and a second client

items.where: Code composer > Model for this agent
steps: Click Code in the sidebar, then New, and look at the composer.
Check the Model for this agent dropdown, shown only when models are offered.
Open the same session in the other client and compare the model shown.
items.needs: an account that can see the Model for this agent dropdown, and a second client
items.note: No code found for sharing instruction files across clients. The E2B gate cited in the plan is about sandbox provisioning, not model or instruction settings.

items.where: Sidebar > Code > open a local session > Session actions (the ... button) > Continue in VS Code or the terminal
steps: Open the Desktop app, click Code, and open a local session.
Click the Session actions button (...) in the header.
Click Continue in VS Code or the terminal.
Look for the Continue in VS Code link and the text To continue in the terminal, run this in the same folder:, with a command below it.
Compare with the Expected line: the hand-off is explicit.
items.needs: the Desktop app with a local session; VS Code is optional for the link

labels.text: Continue in VS Code or the terminal
To continue in the terminal, run this in the same folder:

items.note: Only local sessions show this menu item; cloud sessions show Continue in VS Code in the Changes panel.

items.needs: a phone with the mobile app and the Desktop app
items.note: Desktop side is in Settings > Capabilities > Remote Control (apps/web/features/desktop-host/components/RemoteControlSection.tsx), but I found no phone-side screen for continuing local execution in apps/desktop; the dispatcher line cited is a generic remote control start.

items.needs: a paid account, and cloud execution enabled on the server
items.note: Cloud execution depends on the E2B provisioning gate (apps/web/lib/e2b/gate.ts, e2bProvisioningReady). I could not find a desktop control that continues a cloud session from the local app beyond the shared Code page.

items.needs: a cloud session that produced results, and a local folder
items.note: Searched apps/web/features/code and apps/desktop/electron for return-to-local wording. apps/desktop/electron/windowPolicy.ts:85 only opens external links. The closest control is Apply to local (apps/web/features/code/local-code.ts:1610), which applies a local worktree, not cloud results.

items.where: Sidebar > Your computer
steps: Sign in on a web browser (not the Desktop app, which hides this item).
Click Your computer in the Code sidebar.
Look for the heading Computers on your account and a list of computers.
items.needs: a web browser and a Desktop app linked to the same account

items.where: Settings > Account > Linked devices
steps: Click Settings, then Account.
Scroll to Linked devices.
Find a row for a Desktop app device and read its name, the surface label and its status.
items.needs: a Desktop app linked to the account
items.note: Rows are text lines; I did not confirm a card layout in the code.

items.where: Settings > Account > Linked devices
steps: Click Settings, then Account, and scroll to Linked devices.
Find a device row and read its Can use line.
